before: Routing feedback uses airtime, yet an absent observation may say little about whether a relay forwarded a packet. We examine receipt-assisted passive feedback and the transfer of frozen routing policies to an authenticated transport. A prespecified study comprises 750 IEEE 802.15.4 simulation runs on 30 new fixtures, with active-proof, naive-passive, frozen-prior and capacity-matched policy controls. Under blackholes, delivery rises from 71.28% with active proofs to 75.94% with censored passive feedback: a paired improvement of 4.67 percentage points (95% interval 2.36–6.97; Holm-adjusted p=0.0161). Energy per delivered byte falls, although total modeled radio energy increases slightly. A separate 180-run study evaluates attention, multilayer perceptron and greedy routing with serialized neighbor state, hop authentication, replay protection and signed sink receipts. Attention delivers 81.61% of packets in benign conditions and 61.11% under selective dropping; the paired comparisons do not establish an advantage over either control. Serial-interface tests reveal a receive-time freshness error, corrected before repeat testing. Compiled UART-to-radio bridge firmware runs on four emulated Cortex-M3 boards; neural inference and cryptography execute on the host PC. Each host-policy control delivers ten of ten packets. Post-review 60–300 s stress runs expose early routing-energy exhaustion and increasing service debt. The evidence supports the tested feedback replacement and verifies specific implementation paths. Physical-board operation, measured energy consumption and absolute deadline compliance remain unvalidated.
after: Missing forwarding evidence can reflect packet loss, contention or an unobserved transmission, making feedback design a joint problem of inference and airtime. We benchmark ACK-gated censored passive feedback against active proofs in 750 IEEE 802.15.4 runs on 30 new fixtures, with naive-passive, frozen-prior and capacity-matched policy controls. Under blackholes, delivery increases from 71.28% to 75.94%, a paired gain of 4.67 percentage points (95% interval 2.36–6.97; Holm-adjusted p=0.0161). Energy per delivered byte falls while total modeled radio energy rises slightly. The controls do not establish a unique censoring or attention advantage. A separate 180-run experiment tests frozen policies over authenticated messages and node-local records. Attention delivers 81.61% in benign conditions and 61.11% under selective dropping, without an established advantage over greedy or multilayer-perceptron routing. Serial-interface testing identifies and corrects a receive-time freshness error. Compiled UART-to-radio firmware runs on four emulated Cortex-M3 boards; neural inference and cryptography execute on the host PC. Each host-policy control delivers ten of ten packets. An exploratory 60–300 s extension exposes routing-energy exhaustion and increasing service debt. The contribution is a traceable comparison of feedback mechanisms and transport boundaries; the evidence does not establish sustained operation, physical-board performance, measured energy consumption or absolute deadline compliance.
reason: Sharpen contribution; distinguish the 750-run feedback benchmark, 180-run transport study and post-review stress evidence.
